entries.title: acquire
entries.origin: From Middle English acqueren, borrowed via Old French aquerre, ultimately from Latin acquirō (ad- + quaerō ‘to seek for’), reflecting a sense of seeking and obtaining by effort or addition.

entries.title: advertising
entries.origin: Formed in English from advertise and the suffix -ing, used here to name the activity.

entries.title: algorithm
entries.origin: Borrowed into Medieval Latin from Arabic and later reshaped in European languages under the influence of a Greek word for number.

entries.title: anecdote
entries.origin: Borrowed into English in the late 17th century from French anecdote, ultimately from Greek ἀνέκδοτος “accounts unpublished,” formed from ἀν- “not” + ἔκδοτος “published,” itself from ἐκδίδωμι “I publish” (from ἐκ- “out” + δίδωμι “I give”), with the root ultimately traceable to Proto‑Indo‑European *deh₃-.

entries.title: argue
entries.origin: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French arguer, ultimately from Latin arguere meaning “to declare, show, prove,” and reflecting an inherited Indo‑European root *h₂erǵ-; the word displaced native Old English verbs for reproach and dispute.

entries.title: assert
entries.origin: Borrowed into English via Latin assertus, the perfect passive participle of asserō, from ad “to” + serō “join, range in a row”; the sense developed from laying hands on someone to declare or claim them and so came to mean declare or lay claim to.

entries.title: at odds
entries.origin: From English at + odds, where odds once meant “dissimilarity” or “inequality”; the prepositional phrase developed to denote a state of disagreement or difference.

entries.title: bandwidth
entries.origin: From an English compound of band and width.

entries.title: beta
entries.origin: From Ancient Greek beta, the name of the second letter of the Greek alphabet. English later extended the name to other uses.

entries.title: buck
entries.origin: In American English, buck developed as an informal name for one dollar.

entries.title: bug
entries.origin: From Middle English bugge, used for a beetle-like creature. The technical sense for a fault or error is recorded from the nineteenth century.

entries.title: catch on
entries.origin: Formed in English by combining the verb catch with on.

entries.title: chuckle
entries.origin: Derived from the English verb "chuck" plus the frequentative/inchoative suffix -le, forming a word meaning a quiet or restrained laugh.

entries.title: concierge
entries.origin: Borrowed from French concierge through earlier French forms and medieval Latin consergius. The earlier history is uncertain, though a connection with a Latin expression meaning “fellow servant” has been proposed.

entries.title: crowd
entries.origin: English crowd comes from Middle English crouden, from Old English crūdan and earlier Proto-Germanic *krūdan/*kreudaną, ultimately traceable to a Proto-Indo-European root *grewt- meaning “to push, press.” The word is cognate with Low German kroden and Dutch kruien, reflecting a sense of pressing or pushing together.

entries.title: documentation
entries.origin: From English document plus the suffix -ation, or borrowed via medieval Latin documentātiō denoting the act or result of documenting.

entries.title: elucidate
entries.origin: From Latin ēlūcidātus, the perfect passive participle of ēlūcidō “to lighten, enlighten,” itself formed with the verb-building suffix from ex- + lūcidus “bright, clear.” The Latin word ultimately goes back to Proto-Indo-European *lewk- meaning “bright; to see; to shine.”

entries.title: enthusiasm
entries.origin: Borrowed into English through French and Latin from a Greek word. Its earlier sense described an inspired state; in modern English it means strong excitement or interest.

entries.title: equity
entries.origin: Borrowed into Middle English as equitee (also equytee) from Old French equité, ultimately from Latin aequitas, where it carried the idea of uniformity, impartiality, and fairness.

entries.title: ethnography
entries.origin: Formed in English from ethno- and -graphy.

entries.title: explicate
entries.origin: Borrowed from Latin explicare, meaning “unfold” or “explain”. The figurative sense developed from making something folded clear by opening it.

entries.title: face the music
entries.origin: The origin is uncertain. One proposed explanation connects the expression with a performer facing an orchestra and an audience; this remains a hypothesis.

entries.title: friendliness
entries.origin: From Middle English freendlynesse / frendlynes, formed by adding the noun-forming suffix -ness to the adjective friendly.

entries.title: guide
entries.origin: From Middle English guide, through Old French guide and Provençal guida and guidar, ultimately from a Frankish verb meaning “show the way” or “lead”.

entries.title: immigration
entries.origin: Formed in English from immigrate and the suffix -ion, which forms a noun naming an action or process.

entries.title: in a nutshell
entries.origin: A translation of Latin in nuce. Its history is associated with an account of a long text fitted inside a nutshell, suggesting much information contained in very little space.

entries.title: layover
entries.origin: Formed in English from lay and over.

entries.title: manager
entries.origin: Formed from manage and the suffix -er, which names a person who performs an action.

entries.title: modify
entries.origin: Borrowed through French from Latin modificare, meaning “to regulate” or “limit”.

entries.title: multivariate
entries.origin: Formed in English from multi- and variate.

entries.title: nomenclature
entries.origin: From Classical Latin nōmenclātūra, literally 'a calling by name' (from nōmen "name" + calāre "to call"); it entered English with the sense of a list or system of names used to refer to things. The form is related to the doublet nomenklatura.

entries.title: ontology
entries.origin: Borrowed from modern Latin ontologia, built from Greek elements referring to being and an account or study. English use is recorded from 1663.

entries.title: preclude
entries.origin: Borrowed from Latin praecludere.

entries.title: pull out all the stops
entries.origin: Alludes to organ stops: pulling a stop activates a rank of pipes, so drawing all stops makes the instrument sound as loudly and fully as possible; used figuratively to mean using every available means.

entries.title: serenity
entries.origin: From Middle English serenyte, via Old French serenité, ultimately from Latin serēnitās; formed by adding the adjective-derived -ity to serene and preserving the sense of calmness.

entries.title: squad
entries.origin: Borrowed from French escouade, from Italian squadra, meaning “square”.

entries.title: tax
entries.origin: Borrowed through Old French and Medieval Latin from Latin taxare, meaning “to assess” or “set a charge”.

entries.title: tight
entries.origin: From Middle English forms related to Old English words meaning “dense” or “tight”. The modern spelling was reshaped in Middle English.

entries.title: timetable
entries.origin: Formed in English from time and table.

entries.title: zeal
entries.origin: Inherited in English from Middle English zele, via Old French zel and Late Latin zēlus, ultimately from Greek ζῆλος (zeal, jealousy) and related to a Proto-Indo-European root reconstructed as *yeh₂- ‘to search’.
